article_title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
citation: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910
title: Decision tree used by a curriculum administrator to assess external courses for the Lund C program
description: Based on correspondence with the former program director, the authors constructed a decision tree (Fig. 1) capturing how external courses are assessed for the Lund University Information and Communication Engineering (C) program. "Firstly, the program director decides whether a course is within the scope of the C program, or counted as external." External courses are capped at 15 ECTS; in-scope courses are matched to LU equivalents, assigned a level (G1/G2/A), and possibly counted toward one of five specialization tracks. Partial overlap is credited proportionally: "overlap below 20% (less than 1.5 ECTS) is disregarded; overlap between 20% and 66.7% warrants 2–5 ECTS; and overlap exceeding 66.7% (more than 5 ECTS) is treated as full equivalence." CourseGraph targets the content-overlap decisions in this tree.
requirements: A curriculum administrator's decision process and program metadata (levels, specialization tracks) to ground the assessment rules
constraints: Automatic assignment of course level falls outside the scope of this paper
target_learners: exchange students in the Lund University C program
target_learning_goals: crediting external courses appropriately toward degree requirements
examples: The tree distinguishes external (max 15 ECTS), mandatory-program, and specialization-track outcomes, with five tracks: KS, PVS, PVT, SEC, and ADV
key_sources: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910

article_title: LumiNote: LLM-Assisted Multimodal Instruction for VR Stage Lighting Education
citation: Danxuan Liang, Chun Yin Li, Zheng Wei, Xian Xu, Meng Xia, Huamin Qu, Wai Tong. (2026). LumiNote: LLM-Assisted Multimodal Instruction for VR Stage Lighting Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17335
title: LumiNote: LLM-assisted VR system for stage lighting instruction
description: LumiNote is an instructor-facing LLM-assisted VR system for stage lighting education built on Unity3D and deployed on Meta Quest 3, using GPT-4o and Whisper. It transforms "spoken pedagogical intent into instructor-reviewable spatial annotations, executable demonstrations, and linguistic support" through four modules: scene context serialization, constrained LLM grounding, jargon support, and operational mapping with validation. The system constrains LLM generation along three dimensions: what can be changed, what can be referenced, and how changes are represented.
requirements: Meta Quest 3 headset and Unity3D runtime environment
GPT-4o API access for instruction generation and jargon identification
Pre-defined action schema constraining LLM output to supported operations
constraints: All generated actions remain reviewable and are not executed without instructor approval
Constraints do not guarantee generated actions are technically or pedagogically appropriate
target_learning_goals: Fixture configuration and operation
Spatial lighting behavior
Color theory and visual effects
Composition strategies
key_sources: Danxuan Liang, Chun Yin Li, Zheng Wei, Xian Xu, Meng Xia, Huamin Qu, Wai Tong. (2026). LumiNote: LLM-Assisted Multimodal Instruction for VR Stage Lighting Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17335

article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: LUDIA: a no-cost, private, multilingual AI thought partner grounding educators in UDL
description: LUDIA is a browser-based AI tool for educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders, described as "a no-cost, private, multilingual AI thought partner that connects educators with the Universal Design for Learning framework". Unlike general-purpose chatbots used as solution engines, it is engineered to ground every response in the UDL Guidelines, connect the educator's situation to relevant Guidelines so the reasoning is visible, and offer options to weigh rather than instructions to follow. It relaunches in August 2026 on a purpose-built platform with no accounts, no cookies, and no server-side chat storage.
requirements: Requires a browser and an internet connection; the user must confirm they are 18 or older
constraints: The authors state they hold no evidence that LUDIA improves learning; the relaunched tool has no outcome data, no efficacy trial, and no monitoring because it has not yet been used
Machine-translated languages other than English have not been validated by professional translators and may contain errors
Cost-free is not always-available: the self-funded architecture caps how many educators it can serve at one moment
target_learners: Educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders in schools and learning organisations
target_learning_goals: Identifying and reducing barriers in the design of instruction and learning environments using the UDL Guidelines
examples: Beta tested ahead of relaunch by a global community of volunteer educators in their own planning and design work across languages, education systems, and cultural contexts
key_sources: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en

article_title: Synthesizing frameworks of higher education student learning outcomes
citation: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher
title: Degree Qualifications Profile (DQP)
description: The Lumina Foundation's Degree Qualifications Profile describes what students at any educational level should know and be able to do with a particular degree, with achievement levels defined for associate's, bachelor's, and master's degrees. "the DQP provides descriptions for five areas of learning: broad, integrative knowledge; specialized knowledge; intellectual skills; applied learning, and civic learning". Its descriptors resulted from a review of over a decade of U.S. higher education research.
requirements: Outcomes are defined per degree level, demonstrating how students should perform at increasingly challenging levels
constraints: Outlines the abilities of degree holders, not necessarily prospective employees; the Lumina Foundation notes the five areas overlap in practice and should be integrated
target_learners: associate's, bachelor's, and master's degree students
target_learning_goals: broad integrative knowledge
specialized knowledge
intellectual skills
applied learning
civic learning
examples: Lumina set a goal to increase the proportion of Americans holding high-quality degrees and credentials to 60% by 2025
key_sources: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher

article_title: World Bank Influence on Policy Formation in Education: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725
title: Lukes' three dimensions of power as an analytic lens for international-organization influence
description: The review analyzes its 11 pathways through Lukes' (2005) three dimensions of power: influencing formal decision-making by advancing one's interests; shaping others' preferences or preventing decisions; and using 'social forces and institutional practices' to keep unfavorable issues out of politics and policy. Dale's summary describes the dimensions as the 'naked' use of superior power, the politics of non-decisionmaking such as agenda setting, and control of the 'rules of the game'. The review's key insight is that many pathways contribute to multiple dimensions of power at once, which shows the value of combining Lukes' abstract dimensions with a concrete typology of influence strategies.
requirements: A nuanced typology of concrete influence pathways is needed alongside the power dimensions, since the dimensions alone operate at more abstract levels
constraints: The framework is applied to one international development bank's actions at the national level, not to policy diffusion generally
target_learners: Education policy scholars and researchers of global governance
target_learning_goals: Analyzing how international organizations exercise overt and less overt forms of power in policymaking
examples: The discussion section classifies pathways such as loans, conditionalities, and knowledge production according to the dimension(s) of power they engage
key_sources: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725

article_title: Effects of instructional design, instructional preferences, and cognitive load on problem solving and knowledge acquisition in a computer-based office simulation
citation: Sabrina Ludwig, Andreas Rausch, Michelle Taub. (2026). Effects of instructional design, instructional preferences, and cognitive load on problem solving and knowledge acquisition in a computer-based office simulation. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102255
title: LUCA browser-based office simulation for business learning and assessment
description: LUCA is a browser-based office simulation developed as a learning and assessment environment in business contexts. It "provides learners with typical office tools such as an email client, a file system, a PDF viewer, a spreadsheet application, a calculator, a notepad, and a reduced enterprise resource planning (ERP) system". An integrated authoring environment allows developing and modifying authentic work scenarios, and questionnaires and traditional test items are implemented within it. In this study, all questionnaires, the instructional video, and the 40-min supplier selection problem-solving scenario ran inside LUCA, with log data (mouse clicks and keystrokes) collected during the scenario.
requirements: An integrated authoring environment to develop and modify authentic work scenarios for learning or assessment purposes
constraints: In the reported study, participants worked under individual observation and could not influence the order of the phases
target_learners: undergraduate business and economic education students
target_learning_goals: supplier selection and multi-attribute utility analysis in business education
domain-specific problem solving with typical office tools
examples: Participants received an email task, read two supplier offers, calculated purchase prices, evaluated suppliers in a decision table, and communicated a well-founded decision via email reply
key_sources: Sabrina Ludwig, Andreas Rausch, Michelle Taub. (2026). Effects of instructional design, instructional preferences, and cognitive load on problem solving and knowledge acquisition in a computer-based office simulation. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102255

article_title: Balancing’ privacy and open science in the context of COVID-19: a response to Ifenthaler & Schumacher (2016)
citation: Joshua M. Rosenberg, K. Bret Staudt Willet. (2021). Balancing' privacy and open science in the context of COVID-19: a response to Ifenthaler & Schumacher (2016). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09860-8
title: Lundberg et al.'s (2019) decision-making model for balancing privacy risk to respondents with societal (science) benefits
description: A decision-making model for balancing privacy and open science developed by Lundberg et al. (2019) in the context of the Fragile Families Challenge. Rather than prescribing a recipe, the model is "deeply contextualized" in a project's discipline and risks to participants, and it operationalizes balance as "a tiered system of sharing some data publicly and other data through a gated application system." The commentary presents it as a way to move forward with open science values while respecting participants' privacy and rights, and suggests future work may extend it.
requirements: Sharing decisions must be contextualized in the project, discipline, and understanding of risks to participants rather than following a fixed recipe
constraints: Minimizing participants' risks may require sharing no data while maximizing open science requires sharing all data; the commentary states neither extreme is tenable in many cases
target_learning_goals: ethical data sharing and protection of participant privacy in research and learning analytics
examples: The commentary's authors applied a similar tiered approach in their own work: a carefully anonymized Twitter dataset plus an application process for access to the original data, and Reddit data shared in original form
key_sources: Joshua M. Rosenberg, K. Bret Staudt Willet. (2021). Balancing' privacy and open science in the context of COVID-19: a response to Ifenthaler & Schumacher (2016). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09860-8

article_title: Laparoscopic simulation training improves operating room performance of surgical residents: a multicenter randomized trial (NOVICE).
citation: Thomaschewski M, Vonthein R, Keck T, Laubert T, Benecke C. (2025). Laparoscopic simulation training improves operating room performance of surgical residents: a multicenter randomized trial (NOVICE). International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000002304
title: Lübeck Toolbox (LTB) Curriculum — video-based, goal-directed laparoscopic basic-skills simulation curriculum
description: The LTB Curriculum is "a video training platform with a goal-directed curriculum for the acquisition of basic laparoscopic skills", allowing trainees to practice without an experienced mentor. In the NOVICE trial the intervention group completed it over six weeks between their first and second laparoscopic cholecystectomies, and the trial validated its transferability to the operating room.
requirements: Structured, standardized, goal-directed curriculum content delivered over a scheduled six-week training period
constraints: The study addressed only basic laparoscopic skills, not performance of a complete laparoscopic procedure
target_learners: first-year surgical residents with no prior laparoscopic experience
target_learning_goals: basic laparoscopic skills such as depth perception, bimanual dexterity and instrument handling
examples: In the NOVICE trial, group A completed the LTB curriculum within six weeks while the control group waited without any minimally invasive surgery training
key_sources: Thomaschewski M, Vonthein R, Keck T, Laubert T, Benecke C. (2025). Laparoscopic simulation training improves operating room performance of surgical residents: a multicenter randomized trial (NOVICE). International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000002304

article_title: Acute Stroke Units Nested within Broader Neurology: Care Bundles for Nursing to Enhance Competence and Interdisciplinary Coordination.
citation: Klinke Marianne Elisabeth, Thorarinsson Bjorn Logi, Sveinsson Ólafur Árni. (2025). Acute Stroke Units Nested within Broader Neurology: Care Bundles for Nursing to Enhance Competence and Interdisciplinary Coordination. Current Neurology and Neuroscience Reports. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11910-025-01409-7
title: Four acute stroke nursing care bundles for surveillance at Landspítali University Hospital
description: The article describes four distinct nursing care bundles developed for a small stroke unit: thrombolysis and endovascular treatment, ischemic stroke without recent recanalization therapy, risk of malignant edema and suspected elevated intracranial pressure, and intracerebral hemorrhage. The authors state "We identified a need for four distinct care bundles that, while sharing many common care components, differed in important aspects" and that "Each care bundle comprised four to five essential components, with overlapping elements across all pathways". Common components include position and mobility, fever, sugar, swallowing (FeSS), nutritional intake, neurostatus, and vital signs, with a bleeding-risk component for the thrombolysis bundle and shared red flags for notifying the stroke physician.
requirements: Developed through an interdisciplinary stakeholder forum and a two-tiered staff involvement structure using Borgerts et al.'s method
Designed as worksheets to structure doctors' rounds and documentation in electronic health records
constraints: The article notes bundles are tailored to a four-bed surveillance room within a 22-bed neurological department with a 1:4 nurse-to-patient ratio plus an LPN
target_learners: licensed practical nurses in stroke care
target_learning_goals: structured acute stroke nursing surveillance
timely detection of neurological deterioration
adherence to evidence-based stroke nursing care
examples: Care bundle I transitions patients from thrombolysis/endovascular treatment to the ischemic stroke bundle after 24 h; the hemorrhagic bundle specifies hourly GCS and a systolic blood pressure target of 120–140 mmHg

article_title: Simulation-based teaching versus traditional small group teaching for first-year medical students among high and low scorers in respiratory physiology, India: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Channegowda Nalini Yelahanka, Pai Dinker Ramanand, Manivasakan Shivasakthy. (2025). Simulation-based teaching versus traditional small group teaching for first-year medical students among high and low scorers in respiratory physiology, India: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2025.22.8
title: Low-cost working lung model with surfactant demonstration for simulating obstructive and restrictive lung pathology
description: The intervention used physical models to recreate normal and altered respiratory physiology. A lung model was "constructed using 2 alveolar units, 3 plastic tubes of equal diameter and length, and a 3-way hose connector" with bag-and-mask ventilation. Obstruction was mimicked with gauze narrowing the airway (bronchitis versus bronchial asthma), and a restrictive pattern was simulated by tying a rubber band around an alveolar unit. A soap-solution experiment on a paper clip demonstrated surfactant reducing surface tension.
requirements: Facilitators demonstrated a standardized approach to ensure the same content was delivered across the 3 groups of 20 students
constraints: The demonstration was designed to align with clinical examination demonstration classes for first-year MBBS students on work of breathing and lung compliance
target_learning_goals: understanding lung compliance, work of breathing, and obstructive versus restrictive lung disorders including spirometry findings
examples: A gauze-narrowed airway inserted into one alveolar unit explained why bronchitis does not respond to bronchodilators, in contrast to bronchial asthma
key_sources: Channegowda Nalini Yelahanka, Pai Dinker Ramanand, Manivasakan Shivasakthy. (2025). Simulation-based teaching versus traditional small group teaching for first-year medical students among high and low scorers in respiratory physiology, India: a randomized controlled trial. article_title: Feasibility of focused cardiac ultrasound training for non-cardiologists in a resource-limited setting using a handheld ultrasound machine.
citation: Acheampong Benjamin MD, Starnes Joseph R MD, Parra David MD, Soslow Jonathan H MD, Awuku Yaw A MD, Aliyu Muktar H MD. (2022). Feasibility of focused cardiac ultrasound training for non-cardiologists in a resource-limited setting using a handheld ultrasound machine. Cardiovascular Journal of Africa. https://doi.org/10.5830/CVJA-2022-057
title: Lumify handheld ultrasound probe with Android tablet interface for focused cardiac imaging
description: The Lumify probe (Philips) is a 1–4-MHz single-phased array cardiac transducer with scanning software connected to an Android tablet interface, in which "the transducer performs most of the beam forming, image acquisition and reconstruction processing". The touchscreen supports tap, pinch-to-zoom and swipe functions, and images can be wirelessly transferred to a picture-archiving and communication system. It served as the imaging hardware for the entire training programme.
requirements: Connection to a smart-device display screen and cloud-based application
target_learners: non-echocardiographer clinicians learning focused cardiac ultrasound
target_learning_goals: image acquisition for limited echocardiographic windows
examples: Used by residents at Cape Coast Teaching Hospital to scan 100 consenting patients between July and September 2018
key_sources: Acheampong Benjamin MD, Starnes Joseph R MD, Parra David MD, Soslow Jonathan H MD, Awuku Yaw A MD, Aliyu Muktar H MD. (2022). article_title: Continuing professional development for primary care physicians: a pre-post study on lung point-of-care ultrasound curriculum.
citation: Shitrit Itamar Ben, Shmueli Moshe, Ilan Karny, Karni Ofri, Hasidim Ariel Avraham, Banar Mey Tal, Goldstein Yoav, Wacht Oren, Fuchs Lior. (2024). Continuing professional development for primary care physicians: a pre-post study on lung point-of-care ultrasound curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05985-z
title: Two-day blended lung POCUS continuing professional development curriculum for primary care physicians
description: A curriculum for primary care physicians in a rural, medically underserved region of southern Israel combining remote and in-person components: "recorded lectures, pre-course assessments, hands-on training, post-workshop lectures, and individual practice." Hands-on workshops ran in small groups of up to five PCPs on a simulator and live patients, led by an intensive care physician with 15 years of experience in clinical POCUS.
requirements: PCPs must have access to ultrasound devices in their clinics, as per the study's inclusion criteria
constraints: The assessments were conducted on healthy models rather than sick patients, which the authors note may not encompass real patient challenges
Independent practice sessions between the two workshops were not monitored
Lasting impact was evaluated only at a 10-week follow-up using self-reported data
target_learners: Primary care physicians (specialists/consultants and family medicine residents) with no prior ultrasound training
target_learning_goals: Acquiring standard lung ultrasound images and interpreting normal versus pathological scans
Integrating lung POCUS into daily primary care practice
examples: PCPs received a total of six recorded lectures amounting to five and a half hours, plus six hours of hands-on training in two three-hour sessions
key_sources: Shitrit Itamar Ben, Shmueli Moshe, Ilan Karny, Karni Ofri, Hasidim Ariel Avraham, Banar Mey Tal, Goldstein Yoav, Wacht Oren, Fuchs Lior. (2024). article_title: Changes in attentional resources during the acquisition of laparoscopic surgical skills.
citation: Thomaschewski M, Heldmann M, Uter J C, Varbelow D, Münte T F, Keck T. (2021). Changes in attentional resources during the acquisition of laparoscopic surgical skills. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zraa012
title: Lübeck Toolbox (LTB) laparoscopic training curriculum
description: The LTB curriculum is a simulation-based minimally invasive surgery training programme consisting of "six related exercises: pack your luggage, weaving, Chinese jump rope, triangle cut, hammer cut, and suturing". It is performed in an LTB video box trainer with standard laparoscopic instruments, and learning progress is operationalized by the number of repetitions and duration per repetition needed to reach a defined training criterion. In this study it served as the 5-week training vehicle whose completion freed attentional resources for a concurrent auditory task.
requirements: Defined training criterion with repetitions and duration per repetition as progress measures
constraints: Was used with medical students with no previous experience in laparoscopic surgery
target_learners: medical students with no previous laparoscopic experience
target_learning_goals: basic minimally invasive laparoscopic surgical skills
examples: In this study all 14 participants completed the curriculum within the 5-week programme, with median repetitions to criterion of 30 for luggage and 17 for suturing
key_sources: Thomaschewski M, Heldmann M, Uter J C, Varbelow D, Münte T F, Keck T. (2021). Changes in attentional resources during the acquisition of laparoscopic surgical skills. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zraa012

article_title: Evaluating the influence of music at different sound pressure levels on medical students' performance of standardized laparoscopic box training exercises.
citation: Nees Lisa Katharina, Grozinger Philipp, Orthmann Natalie, Deutsch Thomas Maximilian, Hennigs André, Domschke Christoph, Wallwiener Markus, Rom Joachim, Riedel Fabian. (2021). Evaluating the influence of music at different sound pressure levels on medical students' performance of standardized laparoscopic box training exercises. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02627-6
title: Luebecker Toolbox standardized laparoscopy box-training setup with timed exercises
description: The Luebecker Toolbox is a commercially available laparoscopy training box with an integrated camera connected to a monitor, four standardized modules allowing six different exercises, and associated online didactic videos. In this study three exercises were used — "Pack Your Luggage", "Chinese Jump Rope", and "Weaving" — training instrument handling, hand-eye coordination, and bimanual and crossing instrument use, with performance measured as time to complete each exercise.
requirements: A short oral introduction and one viewing of the instructional video per exercise to standardize the training procedure
Original grasping forceps and a tutor supervising groups of 4–8 participants
constraints: The study did not use virtual reality simulators, so movement tracking and accuracy as part of overall performance could not be recorded
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students at the end of their clinical curriculum (laparoscopic novices)
target_learning_goals: Basic laparoscopic psychomotor skills: instrument handling, hand-eye coordination, bimanual instrument use
examples: 87 students each performed the three exercises in the same order, repeated three times in a row, with completion time recorded per run

article_title: Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students.
citation: Warriner DR, Bayley M, Shi Y, Lawford PV, Narracott A, Fenner J. (2017). Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1058-1
title: Lumped-parameter (zero-dimensional) model of the human circulation as a hydraulic-electrical analogue
description: A lumped-parameter model (LPM) represents the circulation using ordinary differential equations and hydraulic-electrical analogues. "A LPM can elegantly represent the human heart and peripheral circulation as an electrical analogue, with a capacitor (C) representing the elastic property of the large arteries (total arterial compliance) and a resistor (R) representing the frictional loss in the smaller vessels (systemic vascular resistance)." Disease is modelled by parameter changes: increased resistance for hypertension, reduced blood volume for haemorrhagic shock, and reduced left ventricular contractile performance for heart failure.
requirements: Relatively few model parameters which can be related directly to concepts familiar to the clinician; the selected model was validated and previously used to model heart failure severity
constraints: LPMs assume a uniform distribution of pressure, flow and volume within any compartment at any instant in time; the article notes more complex 3D models may become slow and unwieldy and may not add anything over the simple model
target_learning_goals: understanding the dynamics of the cardiovascular system and disease processes such as hypertension, heart failure and haemorrhage
examples: Input variables in Table 1 tune LVEmax, R, C, volume and heartbeat duration to match guideline-defined disease stages; outputs in Table 2 give blood pressure, cardiac output and heart rate per stage
key_sources: Warriner DR, Bayley M, Shi Y, Lawford PV, Narracott A, Fenner J. (2017). Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1058-1
